claim: Sullivan & Cromwell, the Wall Street law firm founded in 1879, was the base of the Dulles brothers' power. John Foster Dulles joined the firm in 1911 and, as counsel to the U.S. delegation at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, helped draft the German-reparations provisions of the Treaty of Versailles; he became a Sullivan & Cromwell partner in 1920 and its head in 1927. Between the world wars the firm sat at the center of the financial network that rebuilt Germany, and Foster kept its Berlin office open — its lawyers signing letters 'Heil Hitler' — until his partners forced its closure in 1935. His younger brother Allen Dulles, also a Sullivan & Cromwell lawyer, went on to run the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA director, 1953–1961) while Foster served as President Eisenhower's Secretary of State (1953–1959) — the brothers holding the overt and covert instruments of U.S. foreign policy at once. In 'The Devil's Chessboard' (2015), journalist David Talbot argues that Allen Dulles — fired by President Kennedy after the 1961 Bay of Pigs failure — was tied to the network behind Kennedy's November 1963 assassination, and notes the irony that Dulles was then named to the Warren Commission that investigated the killing. The Warren Commission's lone-gunman finding and Talbot's counter-thesis are both contested accounts of who killed Kennedy; the firm-and-Dulles history the thesis is built on is documented.
